cards.title: What is a **function**, and what must be true of every input?
cards.body:
A function assigns to each input in its domain exactly one output.

A rule, a table or a graph can define a function. The only requirement is that no input is sent to two different outputs. Two different inputs may share an output.

Example: the pairs $\{(1,5),(2,5),(3,7)\}$ form a function, since each input appears once. The pairs $\{(1,3),(1,4),(2,5)\}$ do not, because the input $1$ has two outputs.

Key idea: "one output per input" is what lets us write $f(x)$ and trust that it names a single number.
cards.searchQuery: function definition one output per input

cards.title: Define the **domain** and the **range** of a function.
cards.body:
The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs the function actually produces.

Unless a problem says otherwise, the domain is every real number for which the rule makes sense: no division by zero and no square root of a negative number.

Example: for $f(x)=x^2$ with domain $\mathbb{R}$, the range is $[0,\infty)$, because a square is never negative.

Watch out: here "range" does not mean the largest value minus the smallest, as it did in statistics. It is the set of outputs that really occur.
cards.searchQuery: domain and range of a function definition

cards.title: How does the **vertical line test** decide whether a graph shows a function of $x$, and why does it work?
cards.body:
A graph shows a function of $x$ exactly when no vertical line meets it more than once.

Why: a vertical line at $x=a$ stands for the single input $a$. Each point where it meets the graph is an output for that input, so two or more hits mean two or more outputs.

Example: the parabola $y=x^2$ passes the test. The circle $x^2+y^2=1$ fails it, since the line $x=0$ meets it at $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$.

Tip: for a table, the same check is simply "look for an input that appears twice with different outputs."
cards.searchQuery: vertical line test function graph

cards.title: Let $f(x)=2x^2-x$. Evaluate $f(3)$ and simplify $f(a+1)$.
cards.body:
$f(3)=15$ and $f(a+1)=2a^2+3a+1$.

Function notation says "put the input wherever $x$ appears." Think of the rule as $f(\square)=2\square^2-\square$.

Example: $f(3)=2(3)^2-3=18-3=15$. For the second, $f(a+1)=2(a+1)^2-(a+1)=2a^2+4a+2-a-1=2a^2+3a+1$.

Watch out: keep parentheses around a substituted expression. Writing $2a+1^2$ instead of $2(a+1)^2$ gives a different, wrong function value.
cards.searchQuery: function notation evaluate f(a+1)

cards.title: Find the domain of $f(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{x-1}}{x-4}$.
cards.body:
$x\ge 1$ and $x\ne 4$, that is $[1,4)\cup(4,\infty)$.

Each trouble spot gives one condition:

1. The square root needs $x-1\ge 0$, so $x\ge 1$.
2. The denominator must not be zero, so $x\ne 4$.

Both conditions must hold at once. The number $4$ lies inside $[1,\infty)$, so it is cut out of the middle, and $\cup$ means "together with".

Tip: list one condition per trouble spot, then keep only the values that satisfy all of them.
cards.searchQuery: domain of function with square root and fraction

cards.title: For $f(x)=x^2-2x$, find the **average rate of change** of $f$ from $x=1$ to $x=4$.
cards.body:
3

The average rate of change of $f$ from $a$ to $b$ is $\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, the slope of the line through the points $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$.

Example: $f(4)=16-8=8$ and $f(1)=1-2=-1$, so the rate is $\dfrac{8-(-1)}{4-1}=\dfrac{9}{3}=3$.

Key idea: it is called "average" because the function may speed up or slow down inside the interval; this one number only summarizes the whole stretch.
cards.searchQuery: average rate of change over an interval

cards.title: Let $f(x)=\begin{cases} x+1 & \text{if } x<0\\ x^2 & \text{if } 0\le x\le 2\\ 5 & \text{if } x>2\end{cases}$. Find $f(-3)+f(2)+f(4)$.
cards.body:
7

A **piecewise function** uses a different formula on each part of its domain. For each input, first decide which condition it meets, then use only that formula.

- $-3<0$, so $f(-3)=-3+1=-2$.
- $0\le 2\le 2$, so $f(2)=2^2=4$.
- $4>2$, so $f(4)=5$.

The sum is $-2+4+5=7$.

Watch out: the conditions must not overlap, or an input would get two outputs and the rule would stop being a function. Check the boundary value (here $x=2$) with care.
cards.searchQuery: piecewise function evaluate cases

cards.title: Why is it false that $f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)$ for every function $f$?
cards.body:
Function notation means "apply the rule to the single input $a+b$"; it is not multiplication, so it does not distribute, and for most functions the two sides differ.

Example: for $f(x)=x^2$, $f(1+2)=f(3)=9$, but $f(1)+f(2)=1+4=5$.

The equation does hold for some special functions, such as $f(x)=mx$, where $f(a+b)=ma+mb$.

Watch out: the same slip appears as $\sqrt{a+b}=\sqrt a+\sqrt b$ and $(a+b)^2=a^2+b^2$. Testing with small numbers exposes each of them.
cards.searchQuery: f(a+b) not equal f(a)+f(b) function notation

cards.title: Define the **composition** $f\circ g$. Which function acts first?
cards.body:
$(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))$: apply $g$ first, then $f$.

The input $x$ must be in the domain of $g$, and the output $g(x)$ must then be in the domain of $f$.

Example: with $f(x)=2x$ and $g(x)=x+3$, $f(g(x))=2(x+3)=2x+6$, while $g(f(x))=2x+3$.

Watch out: composition is usually not commutative, as that example shows. Read $f\circ g$ from the inside out, or right to left.
cards.searchQuery: composition of functions f of g definition
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: For $f(x)=x^2+1$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{x-3}$, find $(f\circ g)(x)$ and its domain.
cards.body:
$(f\circ g)(x)=x-2$ with domain $[3,\infty)$.

Substitute: $f(g(x))=\left(\sqrt{x-3}\right)^2+1=(x-3)+1=x-2$.

Why: the formula $x-2$ would accept any real number, but the composite only exists where the inner function $g$ does, which needs $x-3\ge 0$.

Watch out: always find the domain before simplifying. After simplifying, the restriction from the inner function is no longer visible.
cards.searchQuery: composition domain inner function restriction
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: What is a **one-to-one function**, and how does the **horizontal line test** detect one?
cards.body:
A function is one-to-one when different inputs always give different outputs; on its graph, no horizontal line meets the curve more than once.

Why: a horizontal line at height $c$ collects every input whose output is $c$. If it hits the graph twice, two inputs share an output.

Example: $f(x)=x^2$ fails, since $f(2)=f(-2)=4$. The function $f(x)=x^3$ passes.

Tip: a failing function can often be rescued by shrinking its domain. The same $x^2$ restricted to $[0,\infty)$ is one-to-one.
cards.searchQuery: one-to-one function horizontal line test
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: What is the **inverse function** $f^{-1}$ of a one-to-one function $f$?
cards.body:
$f^{-1}$ undoes $f$: $f^{-1}(y)=x$ exactly when $f(x)=y$.

The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, and its range is the domain of $f$. An inverse exists only when $f$ is one-to-one, so each output can be traced back to a single input.

Example: for $f(x)=2x+1$, $f(3)=7$ and so $f^{-1}(7)=3$.

Key idea: if $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $f$, then $(b,a)$ lies on the graph of $f^{-1}$. Swapping coordinates reflects the graph in the line $y=x$.
cards.searchQuery: inverse function definition reflection y=x
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Which two identities express that $f$ and $f^{-1}$ undo each other? What function do both compositions equal?
cards.body:
$f^{-1}(f(x))=x$ for $x$ in the domain of $f$, and $f(f^{-1}(x))=x$ for $x$ in the domain of $f^{-1}$.

Both compositions equal the **identity function** $\mathrm{id}(x)=x$, which returns its input unchanged.

Why: $f$ sends $x$ to $y$, and $f^{-1}$ sends $y$ straight back to $x$; the round trip changes nothing.

Tip: to check a proposed inverse, test both compositions. For $f(x)=2x+1$ and $g(x)=\frac{x-1}{2}$: $f(g(x))=x-1+1=x$ and $g(f(x))=\frac{2x}{2}=x$.
cards.searchQuery: inverse function composition identity f(f^-1(x))=x
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Find the inverse of $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$, where $x\ne 3$.
cards.body:
$f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3x+1}{x-2}$

Write $y=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$ and solve for $x$:

1. $y(x-3)=2x+1$, so $xy-3y=2x+1$.
2. Collect the $x$ terms: $xy-2x=3y+1$, so $x(y-2)=3y+1$.
3. $x=\dfrac{3y+1}{y-2}$. Rename the input $x$ to get $f^{-1}(x)$.

Check: $f(f^{-1}(x))=\dfrac{2\cdot\frac{3x+1}{x-2}+1}{\frac{3x+1}{x-2}-3}=\dfrac{(6x+2)+(x-2)}{(3x+1)-3(x-2)}=\dfrac{7x}{7}=x$.

Watch out: the variable $x$ appears twice, so you must gather it on one side before factoring it out.
cards.searchQuery: find inverse of fraction function algebraically
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Find the inverse of $f(x)=x^2-4x$ with domain $x\ge 2$, and state the domain of $f^{-1}$.
cards.body:
$f^{-1}(x)=2+\sqrt{x+4}$, with domain $[-4,\infty)$.

Complete the square: $y=x^2-4x=(x-2)^2-4$.

1. $y+4=(x-2)^2$.
2. Because $x\ge 2$, the number $x-2$ is not negative, so $x-2=\sqrt{y+4}$.
3. $x=2+\sqrt{y+4}$; rename to get $f^{-1}(x)=2+\sqrt{x+4}$.

The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$. The lowest value of $f$ is $-4$ at $x=2$, so the range is $[-4,\infty)$.

Watch out: the domain restriction decides the sign of the root. With $x\le 2$ the inverse would be $2-\sqrt{x+4}$.
cards.searchQuery: inverse of quadratic restricted domain complete the square
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Why is it false that $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$?
cards.body:
The $-1$ in $f^{-1}$ marks the inverse function, which undoes $f$; it is not an exponent, and $\frac{1}{f(x)}$ is the reciprocal.

Example: for $f(x)=2x$, the inverse is $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x}{2}$, but the reciprocal is $\frac{1}{2x}$. At $x=4$ they give $2$ and $\frac18$.

Watch out: the number $f(x)^{-1}$, with the exponent outside the parentheses, does mean the reciprocal. Only the symbol $f^{-1}$ with no argument next to it names the inverse function.
cards.searchQuery: inverse function versus reciprocal misconception
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Why does the graph of $y=f(x-2)$ move **right** by 2, not left?
cards.body:
The new function needs $x$ to be 2 larger to receive the same input that $f$ received before, so every point slides 2 units right.

A **horizontal shift** changes the input, so it acts "backwards". A **vertical shift**, $y=f(x)+k$, changes the output and moves the graph up $k$ in the way you would expect.

Example: if the graph of $f$ has a peak at $x=0$, then $f(x-2)$ peaks where $x-2=0$, at $x=2$.

Watch out: $f(x+3)$ moves the graph 3 units to the left, since $x+3=0$ happens at $x=-3$.
cards.searchQuery: horizontal shift f(x-h) right why
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: How does $y=a\,f\big(b(x-h)\big)+k$ transform the graph of $y=f(x)$? Where does a point $(u,v)$ of the old graph go?
cards.body:
$(u,v)\mapsto\left(\dfrac{u}{b}+h,\ a v+k\right)$: scale by $1/|b|$ horizontally and $|a|$ vertically (reflecting if $b<0$ or $a<0$), then shift right $h$ and up $k$.

A **vertical stretch** by $|a|$ multiplies every height by $|a|$. A **reflection** flips the graph: in the $x$-axis when $a<0$, in the $y$-axis when $b<0$.

Why: the new point $(X,Y)$ satisfies $Y=a f(b(X-h))+k$. The inner value $u=b(X-h)$ is an old input, so $X=u/b+h$, and $Y=av+k$ for the old output $v=f(u)$.

Watch out: the inside changes act on $x$ opposite to how they look, and with the form $b(x-h)$ the factor $b$ is applied before the shift $h$.
cards.searchQuery: transformation of graphs a f(b(x-h))+k
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Describe how the graph of $y=-2\sqrt{x+3}+1$ comes from the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.
cards.body:
Shift left 3, stretch vertically by 2, reflect in the $x$-axis, then shift up 1.

Here $a=-2$, $b=1$, $h=-3$, $k=1$. Follow the points of $y=\sqrt x$:

- $(0,0)\mapsto(-3,\,1)$
- $(1,1)\mapsto(-2,\,-1)$
- $(4,2)\mapsto(1,\,-3)$

Check: at $x=1$ the new function gives $-2\sqrt{4}+1=-3$, matching $(1,-3)$. The domain is $[-3,\infty)$.

Tip: move a few easy points through the rule instead of imagining the whole curve; the ordering mistakes show up at once.
cards.searchQuery: graph transformations square root shift stretch reflect
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Define an **even function** and describe the symmetry of its graph.
cards.body:
$f(-x)=f(x)$ for every $x$ in the domain; the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

The domain must also contain $-x$ whenever it contains $x$.

Example: $f(x)=x^4-3x^2$ gives $f(-x)=(-x)^4-3(-x)^2=x^4-3x^2=f(x)$, so it is even. So are $x^2$ and $|x|$.

Why the name: powers $x^n$ with $n$ even are even functions.
cards.searchQuery: even function definition symmetry y-axis
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Define an **odd function** and describe the symmetry of its graph.
cards.body:
$f(-x)=-f(x)$ for every $x$ in the domain; the graph is unchanged by a rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin.

Example: $f(x)=x^3+x$ gives $f(-x)=-x^3-x=-(x^3+x)=-f(x)$, so it is odd. So are $x$ and $x^5$.

Tip: an odd function that is defined at $0$ must have $f(0)=0$, because $f(0)=-f(0)$.
cards.searchQuery: odd function definition rotational symmetry origin
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: The graph of $y=f(x)$ passes through $(2,5)$. Give a point on the graph of $y=3f(x+1)-4$.
cards.body:
$(1,11)$

Choose the new input so that the inside equals the old input: $x+1=2$, so $x=1$.

Then the output follows: $3f(2)-4=3\cdot5-4=11$.

Check with the general rule: $x+1=u$ means $h=-1$ and $a=3$, $k=-4$, so $(2,5)\mapsto(2-1,\ 3\cdot5-4)=(1,11)$.

Watch out: the shift in $x$ is $-1$ (left), not $+1$.
cards.searchQuery: point on transformed graph f(x+1) stretch shift
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: Why is it false that every function is either even or odd?
cards.body:
Most functions are neither: for example $f(x)=x^2+x$.

Check: $f(-x)=x^2-x$. That differs from $f(x)=x^2+x$, so $f$ is not even, and it differs from $-f(x)=-x^2-x$, so $f$ is not odd. At $x=1$: $f(1)=2$ and $f(-1)=0$.

Key idea: an even part and an odd part can be added, as here ($x^2$ is even and $x$ is odd), and the sum has no symmetry of either kind.

Watch out: $2^x$ and $x+1$ are also neither. Only the zero function is both even and odd.
cards.searchQuery: function neither even nor odd example
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions'

cards.title: For $a>0$ and integers $m,n$ with $n\ge 1$, what does $a^{m/n}$ mean?
cards.body:
$a^{m/n}=\left(\sqrt[n]{a}\right)^m=\sqrt[n]{a^m}$: take the $n$-th root, then the $m$-th power.

This definition keeps the exponent laws working: $\left(a^{1/n}\right)^n=a^{1}=a$, so $a^{1/n}$ has to be the $n$-th root.

Example: $27^{2/3}=(\sqrt[3]{27})^2=3^2=9$ and $16^{-3/4}=\dfrac{1}{(\sqrt[4]{16})^3}=\dfrac{1}{2^3}=\dfrac18$.

Tip: take the root first; the numbers stay small.
cards.searchQuery: rational exponent a^(m/n) nth root
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: What is an **exponential function**, and what does its **growth factor** tell you?
cards.body:
$f(t)=a\,b^t$ with $a\ne0$, $b>0$, $b\ne1$; the growth factor $b$ is the number each output is multiplied by when $t$ goes up by 1.

If $b>1$ the function grows; if $0<b<1$ it decays. The number $a$ is the starting value $f(0)$.

Example: growth of 3% per period has $b=1.03$; a loss of 20% per period has $b=0.8$.

Key idea: a linear function adds the same amount each step; an exponential function multiplies by the same factor each step.
cards.searchQuery: exponential function growth factor a b^t
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: A town of 2000 people grows 5% each year. Write a formula for the population $P(t)$ after $t$ years and find $P(10)$, rounded to the nearest person.
cards.body:
$P(t)=2000\,(1.05)^t$ and $P(10)\approx 3258$.

Each year the population is multiplied by $1+0.05=1.05$, so the growth factor is $1.05$ and the starting value is $2000$.

Example: $P(10)=2000\cdot1.05^{10}\approx2000\cdot1.62889\approx3257.8$, which rounds to $3258$.

Watch out: the factor is $1.05$, not $0.05$ and not $5$. A percent increase turns into a multiplier of $1+$ the rate.
cards.searchQuery: exponential growth population 5 percent per year
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: Give the **compound interest** formula for a principal $P$ at annual rate $r$ compounded $n$ times per year for $t$ years.
cards.body:
$A=P\left(1+\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}$

Here $r$ is written as a decimal, and $A$ is the final amount. Each of the $nt$ compounding periods multiplies the balance by $1+\frac{r}{n}$.

Example: $\$1000$ at $6\%$ compounded monthly for 1 year gives $1000(1.005)^{12}\approx\$1061.68$, a little more than the $\$1060$ from simple yearly interest.

Watch out: use $r/n$ per period, not $r$.
cards.searchQuery: compound interest formula P(1+r/n)^(nt)
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: What is the number $e$, and what is its link to compounding?
cards.body:
$e\approx 2.71828$: the value that $\left(1+\frac1n\right)^n$ approaches as $n$ grows without bound.

Compounding $100\%$ interest $n$ times a year gives $\left(1+\frac1n\right)^n$ after a year. This is $2$ for $n=1$, about $2.613$ for $n=12$ and about $2.7169$ for $n=1000$, and it never passes $e$.

Key idea: compounding as often as possible is called continuous compounding, and gives $A=Pe^{rt}$.

Why it matters: $e$ is the base for which exponential growth is simplest to describe, and $e$ is irrational.
cards.searchQuery: number e definition continuous compounding
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: Give the decay formula for a quantity with initial amount $N_0$ and **half-life** $h$.
cards.body:
$N(t)=N_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/h}$

The half-life is the time it takes for the quantity to fall to half its amount. Every time $h$ passes, the amount is multiplied by $\frac12$, so after time $t$ that happens $t/h$ times.

Example: $80$ mg with half-life $3$ days. After $9$ days, $t/h=3$ and $N=80\cdot\frac18=10$ mg.

Tip: the same shape gives doubling time: $N=N_0\,2^{t/d}$ for doubling time $d$.
cards.searchQuery: half-life decay formula N0 (1/2)^(t/h)
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: A deposit of $\$1000$ earns $6\%$ per year compounded continuously. Find the balance after 5 years, to the cent, and compare it with annual compounding at $6\%$.
cards.body:
$1000e^{0.3}\approx\$1349.86$, versus $\$1338.23$ with annual compounding.

For continuous compounding $A=Pe^{rt}$, so $A=1000e^{0.06\cdot5}=1000e^{0.3}$, and $e^{0.3}\approx1.349859$.

For annual compounding $A=1000(1.06)^5\approx1000\cdot1.338226=\$1338.23$.

Key idea: the extra $\$11.63$ is the small gain from compounding at every instant instead of once a year.

Watch out: the product $rt$ must use the rate as a decimal ($0.06$, not $6$).
cards.searchQuery: continuous compounding Pe^(rt) problem
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: Why is it false that after two half-lives a radioactive sample has completely disappeared?
cards.body:
After two half-lives one quarter remains, because each half-life halves whatever is left.

Example: from $100$ g, one half-life leaves $50$ g, two leave $25$ g, three leave $12.5$ g, and so on. The formula $N_0(\frac12)^{t/h}$ gives $N_0(\frac12)^2=\frac14N_0$.

Why: the amount lost in each period is half of what is present, and that shrinks. An exponential decay never reaches exactly zero.

Watch out: this is the same pattern as constant percent growth, only run in reverse.
cards.searchQuery: two half-lives one quarter remains misconception
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: Define the **logarithm** $\log_b x$, for $b>0$, $b\ne1$ and $x>0$.
cards.body:
$\log_b x=y$ exactly when $b^y=x$: the logarithm is the exponent that $b$ must be raised to in order to get $x$.

So a logarithm statement and an exponential statement say the same thing in two forms.

Example: $\log_2 32=5$ because $2^5=32$; $\log_{10}0.001=-3$ because $10^{-3}=0.001$; $\log_9 3=\frac12$ because $9^{1/2}=3$.

Key idea: when stuck on a logarithm, rewrite it as "base to what power gives this number?"

Watch out: $b$ must be positive and not $1$, and $x$ must be positive, since no power of a positive base is zero or negative.
cards.searchQuery: logarithm definition exponent form conversion
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: What are the **common logarithm** $\log_{10}$ and the **natural logarithm** $\ln$?
cards.body:
$\log_{10}x$ is the logarithm with base $10$ (the common logarithm), and $\ln x=\log_e x$ is the logarithm with base $e$ (the natural logarithm).

Example: $\log_{10}1000=3$ because $10^3=1000$, and $\ln e^5=5$.

Why: base $10$ matches our number system, so $\log_{10}$ counts digits and powers of ten. Base $e$ is the one that works most cleanly with growth and decay formulas $Pe^{rt}$.

Watch out: calculators label base 10 as "log" and base $e$ as "ln". Here and in school books we write $\log_{10}$ and $\ln$ so no base is left to guess.
cards.searchQuery: common logarithm natural logarithm ln log10
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: How are $b^x$ and $\log_b x$ related as functions, and what domain does $\log_b x$ have?
cards.body:
They are inverse functions: $b^{\log_b x}=x$ for $x>0$, and $\log_b(b^x)=x$ for all real $x$. The domain of $\log_b x$ is $(0,\infty)$ and its range is $\mathbb{R}$.

Why: the domain and range swap with the inverse. The range of $b^x$ is $(0,\infty)$, so that is the domain of the log. Its graph is the mirror image of the graph of $b^x$ in the line $y=x$.

Example: $\ln(e^7)=7$ and $10^{\log_{10}25}=25$.

Watch out: $\log_b(-4)$ and $\log_b 0$ do not exist as real numbers.
cards.searchQuery: logarithm inverse of exponential domain range
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

cards.title: State the **product rule** for logarithms. What do the quotient and power rules say?
cards.body:
$\log_b(xy)=\log_b x+\log_b y$ for $x,y>0$.

The related rules are $\log_b\!\left(\frac xy\right)=\log_b x-\log_b y$ and $\log_b(x^k)=k\log_b x$.

Why: write $x=b^s$ and $y=b^t$, so $s=\log_b x$ and $t=\log_b y$. Then $xy=b^{s+t}$, and the exponent $s+t$ is the logarithm of $xy$. Multiplying numbers adds their exponents.

Example: $\ln\dfrac{x^3\sqrt y}{z^2}=3\ln x+\tfrac12\ln y-2\ln z$.
cards.searchQuery: product rule logarithms quotient power rule

cards.title: State the **change of base** formula that expresses $\log_b x$ with natural logarithms.
cards.body:
$\log_b x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln b}$

Any base the calculator offers can be used on top and bottom, so $\log_b x=\dfrac{\log_{10}x}{\log_{10}b}$ works too.

Why: set $y=\log_b x$, so $b^y=x$. Take $\ln$ of both sides: $y\ln b=\ln x$, so $y=\frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$.

Example: $\log_2 20=\dfrac{\ln20}{\ln2}\approx\dfrac{2.9957}{0.6931}\approx4.32$.

cards.title: On the pH scale, $\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}[\mathrm{H}^+]$, where $[\mathrm{H}^+]$ is the hydrogen-ion concentration. How many times larger is $[\mathrm{H}^+]$ at pH 3 than at pH 6?
cards.body:
$1000$ times larger.

Since $[\mathrm{H}^+]=10^{-\mathrm{pH}}$, the ratio is $\dfrac{10^{-3}}{10^{-6}}=10^{3}=1000$.

Key idea: on a **logarithmic scale**, each step of one unit means multiplying by a fixed factor (here $10$) instead of adding a fixed amount.

Another example: sound level in decibels is $L=10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ for intensity $I$ and a reference $I_0$, so every $+10$ dB means ten times the intensity.

Watch out: the minus sign flips the direction, so a lower pH means more hydrogen ions.

cards.title: Solve $4\cdot3^x=100$. Give the exact answer and a value rounded to 3 decimal places.
cards.body:
$x=\log_3 25=\dfrac{\ln 25}{\ln 3}\approx 2.930$

1. Isolate the power: $3^x=25$.
2. Rewrite in logarithm form: $x=\log_3 25$.
3. Use change of base: $x=\frac{\ln25}{\ln3}\approx\frac{3.2189}{1.0986}\approx2.930$.

Check: $3^{2.93}\approx25$ and $4\cdot25=100$.

Watch out: divide by 4 first. Taking the logarithm of $4\cdot3^x$ and treating the $4$ as part of the base is a common slip.

cards.title: Solve $\log_2 x+\log_2(x-2)=3$.
cards.body:
$x=4$

1. Combine with the product rule: $\log_2\big(x(x-2)\big)=3$.
2. Rewrite in exponential form: $x(x-2)=2^3=8$.
3. $x^2-2x-8=0$, so $(x-4)(x+2)=0$ and $x=4$ or $x=-2$.

The value $x=-2$ is extraneous: it makes $\log_2 x$ meaningless, since $-2$ is not positive. At $x=4$: $\log_2 4+\log_2 2=2+1=3$.

Watch out: solving can produce roots that are not in the domain of the original equation. Always substitute back.

cards.title: Why is it false that $\log_b(x+y)=\log_b x+\log_b y$?
cards.body:
The logarithm of a sum has no simple rule. The rule turns a product into a sum: $\log_b x+\log_b y=\log_b(xy)$, not $\log_b(x+y)$.

Example: $\log_2(4+4)=\log_2 8=3$, but $\log_2 4+\log_2 4=2+2=4$.

Why: the product rule holds because multiplying powers adds exponents. Adding numbers has no such effect on exponents.

Watch out: two related slips are $\ln(xy)=\ln x\cdot\ln y$ and $\ln\dfrac xy=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln y}$. Both are false; the rules turn a product into a sum and a quotient into a difference.

cards.title: What is a **rational function**, and what is its domain?
cards.body:
A function $f(x)=\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ where $p$ and $q$ are polynomials and $q$ is not the zero polynomial; its domain is every real $x$ with $q(x)\ne0$.

The $x$-intercepts are the inputs where $p(x)=0$ (and $q(x)\ne 0$). The $y$-intercept is $f(0)$, if $0$ is in the domain.

Example: $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x^2-4}$ has domain all real $x$ except $\pm2$, one $x$-intercept at $-1$, and $y$-intercept $f(0)=-\frac14$.

Key idea: a rational function is to polynomials what a fraction is to integers.
cards.searchQuery: rational function definition domain intercepts

cards.title: What is a **vertical asymptote** of a rational function, and where do you find it?
cards.body:
A vertical asymptote is a line $x=a$ that the graph hugs as $x$ gets close to $a$, with $|f(x)|$ growing without bound; it occurs at $x=a$ when $q(a)=0$ but $p(a)\ne0$ in lowest terms.

Near $x=a$ the denominator is tiny while the numerator is not, so the quotient is huge. The sign of the huge value may differ on the two sides of $a$.

Example: $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}$ has the vertical asymptote $x=2$. Close to $2$ on the right $f$ is large and positive; on the left it is large and negative.

Watch out: the graph never crosses a vertical asymptote, because $f$ is undefined there.
cards.searchQuery: vertical asymptote rational function denominator zero

cards.title: When does a zero of the denominator give a **hole** instead of a vertical asymptote?
cards.body:
When the factor $(x-a)$ cancels completely against the numerator, the graph has a hole at $x=a$; if some factor $(x-a)$ remains in the denominator after canceling, there is a vertical asymptote.

Why: after canceling, the function equals a simpler formula that is well-behaved at $a$, but the original is still undefined there. The graph is the simpler curve with one point removed.

Example: $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}=x+1$ for $x\ne1$. This is a line with a hole at $(1,2)$.

Tip: find the hole's height by plugging $a$ into the canceled formula.
cards.searchQuery: hole versus vertical asymptote rational function cancel

cards.title: A rational function has numerator degree $n$ and denominator degree $m$. How do $n$ and $m$ decide its **horizontal asymptote**, which describes its **end behavior**?
cards.body:
If $n<m$ the asymptote is $y=0$; if $n=m$ it is $y=\dfrac{\text{leading coefficient of }p}{\text{leading coefficient of }q}$; if $n>m$ there is no horizontal asymptote.

End behavior means what $f(x)$ does as $x$ becomes very large in size, positive or negative. A horizontal asymptote is a line $y=c$ that the graph approaches there.

Why: far out only the leading terms matter. Dividing top and bottom by $x^m$ leaves $\frac{a_n x^{n-m}+\cdots}{b_m+\cdots}$.

Example: $\dfrac{3x^2+1}{x^2-4x+3}\to 3$, the ratio of $3$ and $1$.

Watch out: when $n=m+1$ the graph follows a slanted line, not a horizontal one.
cards.searchQuery: horizontal asymptote degree rule rational function end behavior

cards.title: List the domain, holes, asymptotes and intercepts of $f(x)=\dfrac{(x-1)(x+2)}{(x+2)(x-3)}$.
cards.body:
Domain $x\ne-2,3$; hole at $\left(-2,\tfrac35\right)$; vertical asymptote $x=3$; horizontal asymptote $y=1$; $x$-intercept $1$; $y$-intercept $\tfrac13$.

1. The denominator is zero at $x=-2$ and $x=3$, so these are excluded.
2. The factor $x+2$ cancels, leaving $\frac{x-1}{x-3}$. That gives a hole at $x=-2$ of height $\frac{-3}{-5}=\frac35$.
3. The factor $x-3$ remains, so $x=3$ is a vertical asymptote.
4. Degrees are equal with leading coefficients $1$ and $1$, so $y=1$.
5. $x$-intercept: $x-1=0$. $y$-intercept: $f(0)=\frac{-1}{-3}=\frac13$.

Tip: factor first, cancel next, then read every feature from the reduced form.
cards.searchQuery: rational function features hole asymptote intercepts example

cards.title: Solve $\dfrac{2x-1}{x+3}<1$.
cards.body:
$-3<x<4$, that is $(-3,4)$.

Do not multiply by $x+3$: its sign is unknown. Instead move everything to one side:

$\dfrac{2x-1}{x+3}-1=\dfrac{(2x-1)-(x+3)}{x+3}=\dfrac{x-4}{x+3}<0$.

A **sign chart** records the sign of each factor on the intervals cut out by the zeros of the numerator and denominator ($x=4$ and $x=-3$):

- $x<-3$: $(-)/(-)=+$
- $-3<x<4$: $(-)/(+)=-$
- $x>4$: $(+)/(+)=+$

We want negative values, so the answer is $(-3,4)$. Both endpoints are excluded: $-3$ is outside the domain, and $4$ gives $0$, which is not less than $0$.

Check: $x=0$ gives $-\frac13<1$.
cards.searchQuery: solve rational inequality sign chart

cards.title: Find the asymptotes and intercepts of $f(x)=\dfrac{3x^2+1}{x^2-4x+3}$.
cards.body:
Vertical asymptotes $x=1$ and $x=3$; horizontal asymptote $y=3$; no $x$-intercepts; $y$-intercept $\tfrac13$.

1. $x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)$. The numerator at $1$ is $4$ and at $3$ is $28$, neither $0$, so nothing cancels and both zeros give vertical asymptotes.
2. The degrees are equal, with leading coefficients $3$ and $1$, so $y=3$.
3. $3x^2+1\ge1>0$ for all real $x$, so the numerator never vanishes: there are no $x$-intercepts.
4. $f(0)=\frac13$.

Watch out: always test the numerator at each denominator zero; a zero there means a hole, not an asymptote.
cards.searchQuery: asymptotes and intercepts of rational function problem

cards.title: Why is it false that a graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote?
cards.body:
A horizontal asymptote describes what happens far from the origin only; at moderate $x$ the graph may cross it, even more than once.

Example: $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ has horizontal asymptote $y=0$ (numerator degree below denominator degree), yet $f(0)=0$, and $f$ is negative for $x<0$ and positive for $x>0$, so the graph crosses $y=0$ at the origin.

Key idea: a vertical asymptote can never be crossed, since $f$ is undefined there. A horizontal one is only about the ends.
cards.searchQuery: graph can cross horizontal asymptote misconception

cards.title: What is a **mathematical model**, and what is a **parameter** of a model?
cards.body:
A mathematical model is a function or equation that describes a real situation in a simplified way; a parameter is a number in the model that is fixed to fit the situation, such as $a$ and $b$ in $f(t)=a\,b^t$.

A model keeps what matters and ignores the rest, so it is never perfectly accurate.

Example: a car worth $\$20000$ that loses $15\%$ of its value each year has value $V(t)=20000(0.85)^t$ after $t$ years. Here $t$ is the input, and $20000$ and $0.85$ are the parameters.

Key idea: fitting a model means choosing the parameters, such as the starting amount and growth factor, so that the model matches the data.

cards.title: What are the steps of the **modeling cycle**?
cards.body:
Formulate, compute, interpret, validate, report; and if validation fails, go round again.

1. Formulate: choose the quantities and the kind of function to describe them.
2. Compute: fit the parameters and solve the equations.
3. Interpret: say what the answers mean in the situation, with units.
4. Validate: compare with data or common sense.
5. Report: state the result, the assumptions and the limits.

Why: the model's first guess is rarely right. A failed check sends you back to formulate with a better kind of function.

Watch out: a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question if the interpretation step is skipped.

cards.title: Given a table of outputs at equally spaced inputs, how do a **constant difference** and a **constant ratio** tell you the type of model?
cards.body:
Constant differences between consecutive outputs mean a linear model; constant ratios mean an exponential model.

Why: a line $y=mx+c$ adds $m$ for every step, so differences are constant. An exponential $y=ab^x$ multiplies by $b$ each step, so ratios are constant.

Example: outputs $3,7,11,15$ have differences $4,4,4$, so $y=4x+3$. Outputs $5,10,20,40$ have ratios $2,2,2$, so $y=5\cdot2^x$.

Tip: if the differences themselves have a constant difference, a quadratic model is likely.

cards.title: The outputs at $x=0,1,2,3,4$ are $1,2,5,10,17$. Choose between a linear, quadratic or exponential model and find the rule.
cards.body:
Quadratic: $y=x^2+1$.

Differences: $1,3,5,7$, not constant. Ratios: $2,\,2.5,\,2,\,1.7$, not constant. But the differences of the differences are $2,2,2$, which are constant.

For $y=ax^2+bx+c$: $c=y(0)=1$; $y(1)=a+b+1=2$ and $y(2)=4a+2b+1=5$. These give $a+b=1$ and $2a+b=2$, so $a=1$, $b=0$.

Check: $x=4$ gives $16+1=17$.

Watch out: differences that grow are not enough for an exponential model; check the ratios.

cards.title: An exponential model $f(t)=a\,b^t$ passes through $(1,6)$ and $(3,54)$ with $b>0$. Find $f(t)$ and say what $a$ and $b$ mean.
cards.body:
$f(t)=2\cdot3^t$: the starting value is $a=2$ and the quantity triples each step ($b=3$).

1. Divide the two conditions: $\dfrac{ab^3}{ab^1}=\dfrac{54}{6}$, so $b^2=9$, and $b=3$ since $b>0$.
2. Then $a\cdot3=6$, so $a=2$.

Check: $f(1)=6$ and $f(3)=2\cdot27=54$.

Key idea: dividing the equations cancels the unknown $a$ and leaves a single equation for $b$.

Watch out: the starting value is $f(0)=2$, not the first data point $6$.

cards.title: A rectangular pen has perimeter $40$ m. Model its area as a function of the width $w$, state a sensible domain, and find the largest area.
cards.body:
$A(w)=w(20-w)$ with domain $0<w<20$; the largest area is $100\ \mathrm{m^2}$ at $w=10$.

1. Perimeter $2w+2\ell=40$, so the length is $\ell=20-w$.
2. Area $A=w\ell=w(20-w)=-w^2+20w$.
3. Both sides must be positive: $w>0$ and $20-w>0$.
4. The parabola opens downward, so its vertex is the maximum, at $w=-\frac{20}{2(-1)}=10$, giving $A=10\cdot10=100$.

Interpret: the best rectangle is a square of side $10$ m.

Watch out: the algebra of $A(w)$ is fine for $w=25$, but a negative length makes no sense. The domain comes from the situation, not the formula.

cards.title: Why is it false that a model which fits the data well can be trusted for any input?
cards.body:
A model is only reliable on the range where it was checked and where it makes sense; far outside that range it can give impossible values.

Example: bacteria counted as $N(t)=500\cdot2^t$ for the first few hours fit well. But at $t=200$ hours it predicts about $8\times10^{62}$ cells, far more than there is food, space or matter for.

Why: real growth runs into limits that the simple formula leaves out.

Tip: write the domain of the model next to the formula, and say which part of the data it was fitted to.
